resources.name: ORCID
resources.summary: Free, persistent identifier for individual researchers, maintained by a global not-for-profit; records can be created, edited and maintained free of charge and integrate with journal submission systems, funder and grant application systems, repositories and research information systems.
resources.access: Register at orcid.org, add works and affiliations, then supply the iD in every manuscript, dataset deposit and grant form. A free public API is available for reading records.
resources.notes: Costs nothing to individuals; the paid membership tiers are for institutions and publishers integrating the API. For unaffiliated researchers this is the single cheapest piece of infrastructure that makes a publication record portable and machine-readable — it disambiguates you from name-alikes and survives every change of institution or none at all.

resources.name: 1517 Fund — Medici Project
resources.subcategory: no-strings micro-grants for students and dropouts
resources.summary: Micro-grants of at least $1,000, paid with no strings attached, to high-school and college students, dropouts and deep-tech scientists working on a self-directed project — explicitly not projects done for grades or admissions.
resources.access: Email any team member at firstname@1517fund.com with a five-minute Loom video: who you are, why you care about the project, and what the money unlocks.
resources.notes: Effectively North America only — the fund states international applicants may get limited support because of regulatory constraints. Amounts are small and this is a talent-scouting pipeline for a venture fund, so expect the framing to favour buildable artefacts over scholarly output.

resources.name: ACL Diversity & Inclusion and virtual subsidies
resources.summary: The Association for Computational Linguistics runs D&I subsidies and separate virtual-attendance subsidies for its main conference; both calls were announced for ACL 2026 (April 2026).
resources.access: Calls are posted on each year's conference site with their own forms and deadlines; the virtual subsidy is the low-friction option when travel is impossible.
resources.notes: Amounts, eligibility and deadlines are set fresh each year by that year's D&I chairs and are not stable across conferences — read the specific call rather than a previous year's terms. Sibling conferences (EMNLP, NAACL, EACL) run comparable schemes under the same umbrella.

resources.name: ACX Grants
resources.summary: Grant rounds run by Scott Alexander on the Astral Codex Ten blog, funding individual projects across science, public health, forecasting and software. Results posts confirm rounds in 2021, 2022 (Grants++), 2024 and 2025; the most recent results post is 'ACX Grants Results 2025' (13 October 2025).
resources.access: Rounds are announced as blog posts with a Google Form; watch the blog or subscribe to the RSS feed. Past rounds also ran an associated impact market / mini-grants track.
resources.notes: Cadence is irregular and there is no standing application portal — no open round was visible on the blog as of 2026-08-28, and a June 2025 post ('Open Questions For Future ACX Grants Rounds') suggests the format is still being reconsidered. Grants are small and one-off; the strongest secondary benefit is visibility to the blog's donor-heavy readership.

resources.name: Africa Research Excellence Fund (AREF)
resources.subcategory: career-development fellowships for African health researchers
resources.summary: UK-registered charity, with offices in The Gambia and London, funding early-career African health researchers: Research Development Fellowships have placed 83 fellows at 17 research centres in Africa, Europe and beyond, alongside leadership programmes and grant-writing workshops including a stream for women scientists. AREF reports investing over GBP 3M in 500 researchers who went on to win more than GBP 10M from other funders.
resources.access: Apply to a specific call listed on the Funding Calls page; open on 2026-08-28 were the AREF-MRC Towards Leadership Programme 2026/2027 and a French-language essential grant-writing skills course for January/March 2027.
resources.notes: Amounts and durations are published per call rather than centrally, so the individual call document is the only reliable source. Scope is health and biomedical research by researchers based in Africa — no other regions or disciplines. Most schemes assume an institutional base in Africa and, for placement fellowships, a named host laboratory, so a fully unaffiliated applicant will struggle.

resources.name: AIMS (African Institute for Mathematical Sciences)
resources.subcategory: fully funded master's in mathematical sciences
resources.summary: An intensive one-year postgraduate structured master's in mathematical sciences taught across three semesters by visiting lecturers, run on a full-scholarship model within a pan-African student community.
resources.access: Apply through the AIMS prospective-students pages; the network operates centres in several African countries, each with its own intake.
resources.notes: What the scholarship covers in detail (tuition, accommodation, meals, travel) is not stated on the programme pages checked on 2026-08-28 — email the centre and get it in writing before you commit. Intake is aimed at African graduates in mathematical sciences; the pace is demanding and the programme is residential.

resources.name: Astera Residency
resources.summary: A 12–18 month fully funded residency for people building public-goods research projects in neuroscience, AI, AI-enabled life sciences and open science: salary of $125,000–$250,000 depending on experience, a project budget of up to $1.5M, and compute access via Voltage Park (24,000 NVIDIA H100s plus reserved B200/GB300 capacity).
resources.access: Open online application when a cycle is live; cycles run roughly twice a year, so check the residency page periodically.
resources.notes: Residents work in person at Astera's Emeryville, California hub, which means relocation and a US work authorisation problem for most international applicants. Outputs must be committed to open and accessible release. Extremely competitive and scoped to Astera's focus areas — a strong track record is assumed.

resources.name: Breakthrough Junior Challenge
resources.summary: Annual global science-video competition for high-school students, with a $250,000 post-secondary scholarship for the winner, a $50,000 prize for their teacher and a $100,000 Breakthrough Science Lab for their school. The current cycle closes 15 September 2026 (peer review due 30 September 2026).
resources.access: Submit a short explanatory video on a physics, life-sciences or mathematics concept through the challenge site; entrants must also complete a peer-review round on other submissions.
resources.notes: High-school students only — this is not a route for graduate students or independents, and it is included here because it is one of the very few genuinely open, genuinely large science prizes. Single winner per year against a global field, so odds are extremely long.

resources.name: Chevening Scholarships
resources.summary: UK government scholarship scheme funding one-year master's degrees in the UK for candidates from a long list of eligible countries and territories, covering tuition, living costs and travel.
resources.access: Single online application through chevening.org during the annual window (typically opening in August and closing in early November for entry the following autumn); you apply to Chevening and to universities separately.
resources.notes: Requires prior work experience and a commitment to return to your home country after the degree; eligible countries change year to year, so check the country list rather than assuming. Selection weights leadership and career trajectory heavily, not just academic record. The scheme did not respond to automated checks on 2026-08-28 — confirm current dates and the country list on the site.

resources.name: CIMPA
resources.summary: International association that has spent nearly fifty years running mathematics research schools in developing countries, alongside Partnership Schools, CIMPA Fellowships and CIMPA–ICTP Research in Pairs.
resources.access: Two routes: propose and organise a school through the organisers' candidacy portal, or apply as a participant to a specific school listed on the site.
resources.notes: CIMPA's money mainly goes to the organisers of a school, who then decide participant support — whether your travel and local costs are covered depends on the individual school, so ask its organisers directly. Site content is partly in French. Mathematics and mathematical-sciences focus.

resources.name: Code for Science & Society Event Fund
resources.summary: Community-governed fund that invests directly in events building data-science skills and social infrastructure in under-served communities; past cohorts funded open-science training, teacher data literacy and infectious-disease research meetings.
resources.access: Application through the call published on the Event Fund page; CS&S also acts as a fiscal sponsor for open-science projects.
resources.notes: Grant amounts and the current round status are not stated on the landing page — the live call linked as of 2026-08-28 was themed 'Pushing the Boundaries of Research Software Engineering', so scope changes between cohorts. This funds events and community-building, not personal research time.

resources.name: Commonwealth Scholarships (CSC UK)
resources.summary: UK government scheme awarding around 800 postgraduate and professional-development awards a year: Master's Scholarships, PhD Scholarships for least developed countries and vulnerable states, Shared Scholarships, and Commonwealth Fellowships and Startup Fellowships launching from 2026/27. The LDC PhD award covers approved return airfare, full tuition fees agreed directly between the CSC and the UK university, a stipend of GBP 1,712 a month (GBP 2,000 in the London metropolitan area), and study-travel and fieldwork grants.
resources.access: Applications go through the CSC Central online portal, but only via a nominating body — a national nominating agency, a UK university, or a listed non-governmental or charitable body. The CSC does not accept direct applications.
resources.notes: The nominating-body gate is the binding constraint: if your country's agency is not nominating this cycle there is no way in, whatever your record. Country eligibility is per scheme — the LDC PhD list is 17 countries (Bangladesh, The Gambia, Kiribati, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Nigeria, Pakistan, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, Solomon Islands, Sri Lanka, Tanzania, Togo, Tuvalu, Uganda, Zambia). Applicants must declare they could not otherwise afford to study in the UK. Windows differ by scheme; the LDC PhD page listed 8 September to 20 October 2027 (16:00 BST) for its next round on 2026-08-28.

resources.name: DAAD Scholarship Database
resources.summary: Free, filterable database of scholarships for international students, graduates and researchers coming to Germany, showing 149 scholarship options in the English interface, filterable by your country of residence, status and subject.
resources.access: Web interface, no account needed — set your country of residence and status, then read each programme's own terms and deadline.
resources.notes: The country filter refers to where you currently live and apply from, not your nationality; DAAD advises contacting them if you are applying from elsewhere. The database also indexes non-DAAD funders, whose entries DAAD does not guarantee — check terms with the programme itself. Monthly stipend amounts are on the individual programme pages, not the search results.

resources.name: Dimensions (free version)
resources.summary: Free personal-use tier of the Dimensions database: more than 140 million publications and 29 million datasets, with records linked to the grants, clinical trials, patents and policy documents that fund or cite them. It is the broadest free route to see which funder paid for a given paper outside the US-only NIH RePORTER and NSF Award Search.
resources.access: Free account at app.dimensions.ai — full-text search with filters for researcher, source title, category and open-access status, plus export, ORCID linking and reference saving via ReadCube.
resources.notes: The free tier is licensed for personal, non-commercial use only. Grants appear as linked context on publication records rather than as a fully searchable and analysable grants database — that, and the institutional analytics, sit behind the paid tier, so this does not replace a real grants search for a funder you already know. Funder coverage is strongest for large English-language funders and thin for national agencies in the Global South.

resources.name: DrivenData
resources.summary: Machine-learning competitions with social-impact sponsors including NASA, Microsoft, Meta AI and the World Bank. Open competitions as of 2026-08-28 include Trace the Ace ($50,000 in prizes), Lost in Transcription ($20,000) and the DaT Parkinson's Challenge (€25,000).
resources.access: Register, download the competition data, and submit predictions against the leaderboard; practice competitions with no prizes are available for learning.
resources.notes: Fewer, longer competitions than Kaggle, which means less crowding but also fewer chances per year. Prize eligibility, licensing of winning code and any country restrictions are set per competition — read the individual rules. Winning solutions are usually required to be open-sourced, which is a plus for a public record but a constraint if you wanted to commercialise.

resources.name: EA Funds — Transformative AI Fund
resources.summary: Always-open fund making grants typically in the $10k–$150k range (rarely above $300k) to individuals, new organisations and existing organisations starting a new project, explicitly aiming to be 'early-stage, fast, and tolerant of failure'.
resources.access: Rolling online application form on the fund page; contact transformativeai [at] effectivealtruismfunds.org with questions.
resources.notes: This fund replaced the Long-Term Future Fund, which EA Funds closed — old LTFF links now redirect here, so guides that still name the LTFF are out of date. Scope is restricted to work on risks and impacts from transformative AI; a general independent-research salary request outside that scope will not fit.

resources.name: EMBO Postdoctoral Fellowships
resources.summary: Up to two years of support for life-science postdocs, providing a salary or stipend, a relocation allowance, support for fellows with children, and a place on an EMBO Laboratory Leadership course. Applications are accepted year-round against periodic hard deadlines; the next is Friday 22 January 2027, 14:00 CET.
resources.access: Direct online application by the candidate through the EMBO portal, with the agreement of the proposed host laboratory. No application fee.
resources.notes: International mobility is a hard requirement, and you need at least one first-author peer-reviewed paper or accepted refereed preprint, so this is not a route straight out of a thesis with nothing published. From the Autumn 2026 round a single host laboratory may back only one candidate per selection round, and from Autumn 2027 re-application is barred entirely — one submission per researcher, ever. Stipend amounts are set per host country and are not published as one global figure.

resources.name: EMBO Scientific Exchange Grants
resources.summary: Grants funding research exchanges of up to three months between laboratories in EMBO-eligible countries, covering the visiting researcher's travel and subsistence at published rates. Applications are accepted throughout the year with no fixed deadline.
resources.access: Online application on the EMBO site at any time; download the guidelines plus the subsistence-rate and travel-allowance documents before setting a budget, since the rates are fixed per country.
resources.notes: Eligibility is defined by country pairs — both your home and host country must be on EMBO's eligible list — so check the eligibility page first, because most refusals here are structural rather than scientific. It funds the visit only: no salary at home, no consumables, no bench fees. This is the lowest-friction EMBO route for a researcher with no travel budget who needs to learn a technique or start a collaboration.

resources.name: Emergent Ventures
resources.summary: Rolling grant programme at the Mercatus Center (George Mason University) for individuals with a specific project; the only stated eligibility bar is being 13 or older, and applicants worldwide are accepted, with dedicated tracks for India, Africa, the Caribbean and Ukraine selectable on the form.
resources.access: Single web application form linked from the programme page; a short project description plus a CV. No institution, no budget template, no letters of reference.
resources.notes: Grant sizes are not published; historically they run from a few thousand dollars to low six figures, and the programme does not publish decision rates or deadlines. Decisions are made by one person and are idiosyncratic — treat it as a lottery ticket with a very cheap ticket, not a plan. No progress reports are required, but also no support structure.

resources.name: Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters
resources.summary: EU-funded catalogue of 220 joint master's programmes delivered by consortia across several countries, with scholarships available for students from anywhere in the world.
resources.access: Search the catalogue, then apply directly to the consortium running the programme you want — applications typically run October to January for the following academic year, and each consortium sets its own process.
resources.notes: The catalogue is updated annually and not every listed programme still carries EU scholarships — some are at the end of their funding period or have kept the Erasmus Mundus name after funding ended, so confirm scholarship availability with the consortium before applying. What the scholarship covers varies by programme. Multi-country study means multiple visa processes.

resources.name: Ethereum Foundation Ecosystem Support Program
resources.summary: Grant programme funding free and open-source public goods for the Ethereum ecosystem, including cryptography, protocol and applied-security research. Published allocations: 677 projects / $44.4M in 2024, 498 / $61.1M in 2023, 397 / $30.0M in 2022.
resources.access: Apply through the Wishlist and RFP listings on the ESP site; a non-financial 'Office Hours' track gives feedback on project ideas before you apply.
resources.notes: Domain-restricted: your work has to plausibly benefit Ethereum, so this suits cryptography, distributed systems, formal methods, mechanism design and privacy researchers and nobody else. Individual grant sizes are not published. Payment is often in crypto, which creates tax and accounting work.

resources.name: EU Funding & Tenders Portal
resources.summary: Single entry point for European Union funding calls, including Horizon Europe, the European Research Council and Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions, with full call documents, work programmes and evaluation criteria published openly.
resources.access: Browse and search calls without logging in; an EU Login account and a participant identification code are required to submit a proposal.
resources.notes: Almost all calls require a legal-entity applicant, usually with a host organisation, so an unaffiliated individual cannot submit alone. The portal is dense and the terminology is its own dialect — start from the topic's work programme document. Reading past evaluation criteria and funded-project abstracts here is free competitive intelligence even if you never apply.

resources.name: EURAXESS
resources.subcategory: research job, funding and hosting database (Europe)
resources.summary: European Commission portal carrying what it describes as the largest database of research job, funding and hosting offers in Europe, operating across 43 European countries and 9 worldwide hubs; 7,698 offers were listed on 2026-08-28, filterable by offer type (job / funding / hosting), country, 300+ research fields, researcher profile R1-R4 and funding programme (Horizon Europe, Erasmus+ and others).
resources.access: Web interface — search and read any offer without logging in; a free account only adds saved searches and email alerts for new or expiring offers. You then apply to the host institution named in the offer, not to EURAXESS.
resources.notes: Listings are posted by institutions, so completeness and quality vary and expired offers linger in results. Most funding entries assume a European host organisation, and the portal awards nothing itself — it is an index. Non-European researchers can use it freely, but many indexed schemes carry mobility or residency conditions set by the underlying funder, not visible in the search summary.

resources.name: Experiment
resources.summary: Crowdfunding platform built specifically for scientific projects: a researcher publishes a hypothesis, method and itemised budget, and backers fund it directly. It is one of the very few funding routes that does not ask what institution you are at.
resources.access: Web interface — draft a project, pass editorial review, then run a time-limited campaign and drive your own traffic to it.
resources.notes: The platform deducts a percentage fee plus payment processing from funds raised; the fee pages returned HTTP 403 to automated checks on 2026-08-28, so read the current terms yourself before you set a target. Success is a function of the audience you already have — campaigns without an existing mailing list, lab network or press hook routinely fail, and typical raises are in the low thousands, not grant-scale.

resources.name: Falling Walls Lab
resources.subcategory: pitch competition with travel to a global final
resources.summary: Three-minute pitch competition for students and early-career professionals across all disciplines, run as dozens of local Labs worldwide; 100 Lab winners advance to the Global Finale in Berlin each November to compete for the Emerging Talents Breakthrough title.
resources.access: Apply to a local Lab in your region through the Lab locations page; each Lab sets its own deadline.
resources.notes: Whether travel and accommodation to Berlin are covered is set by the organisers of each individual Lab and by the central programme — confirm with your local Lab before assuming a funded trip. The payoff is visibility and network rather than research money.

resources.name: Foresight Institute Fellowship
resources.summary: Year-long fellowship for early-career scientists and engineers in secure AI, longevity biotechnology, nanotechnology, neurotechnology, space and 'existential hope', providing introductions to senior scientists, funders and mentors, paid travel to one technical workshop and one Vision Weekend, seminar-group membership with presentation slots, priority access to Foresight's AI Nodes in San Francisco and Berlin, and quarterly career calls.
resources.access: Open application on the fellowship page; on 2026-08-28 applications were open for the 2028 cohort, with no deadline published. Third-party nominations of candidates are also accepted; questions to fellowship@foresight.org.
resources.notes: No stipend or research budget is disclosed — the value is network and travel, not salary, so it does not replace income. Focus areas are narrow and the community skews toward Bay Area / Berlin technologists.

resources.name: Fulbright Foreign Student Program
resources.summary: US government programme funding non-US citizens to undertake graduate study or research in the United States; applications are made in your home country rather than centrally.
resources.access: Apply to the Fulbright Commission/Foundation or the US Embassy in your home country — the central site's role is to route you to your national commission, which publishes its own deadlines, quotas and terms.
resources.notes: What is funded, how many awards exist and when applications close all vary by country, so a figure quoted for one country tells you nothing about yours. Many national programmes carry a two-year home-residency requirement after the award. US federal funding for exchange programmes has been volatile in recent years; confirm the current cycle with your national commission before building plans around it.

resources.name: GitHub Sponsors
resources.subcategory: recurring support for research software maintainers
resources.summary: Recurring or one-off sponsorship of open-source maintainers, with 103 regions supported globally as stated on the Sponsors page. GitHub charges no fee on sponsorships from personal accounts, so 100% reaches the developer; sponsorships from organisation accounts carry up to 6% (3% credit-card processing, which invoiced billing removes, plus a 3% GitHub service fee).
resources.access: Enable a Sponsors profile on your GitHub account, add sponsor tiers, and surface the Sponsors button on your repositories; payouts go to a bank account or Stripe Connect in a supported region.
resources.notes: You must reside in a supported region to receive funds, which excludes a number of countries. The GitHub Sponsors Matching Fund is closed (applications after 1 January 2020 are not eligible), so there is no longer a match. Realistic income for a scientific package with a small user base is tens of dollars a month; this funds coffee and CI, not a salary, unless the project is widely depended on.

resources.name: Google Summer of Code
resources.summary: Paid, mentored programme placing newcomers on open-source projects for a 12+ week engagement, with project sizes of roughly 90, 175 or 350 hours; many participating organisations are scientific software communities. Stipends are paid on passing evaluations.
resources.access: Pick a participating organisation, engage with its mentors before the window, then submit a project proposal through the GSoC site during the contributor application period.
resources.notes: Open to anyone 18+ who is a student OR an open-source beginner (fewer than about ten prior contributions), eligible to work in their country of residence, and accepted at most once before; residents of US-embargoed countries are excluded. Stipend amounts vary by project size and country tier and are not published on the FAQ — check the current programme rules. Competition for slots at popular organisations is heavy and proposals written without prior contact with mentors rarely succeed.

resources.name: Grand Challenges
resources.summary: Family of open funding calls started by the Gates Foundation in 2003 and now run with government, foundation and nonprofit partners on four continents; partners have collectively funded more than 4,300 projects in more than 120 countries. Calls are topic-specific with their own deadlines — 2026 examples include AI-Enabled Consumer Engagement to Advance Family Planning (21 July 2026) and Innovations in Decentralized Pan-Orthoebolavirus Diagnostics (6 July 2026). The historic Grand Challenges Explorations line (2007-2020) made $100,000 seed grants on short applications.
resources.access: Browse the challenges list and apply to a specific call through the portal linked from that call; proposals are typically short and are reviewed without requiring preliminary data.
resources.notes: Every call sets its own eligibility, and most require a legal entity able to receive and account for funds, so an unaffiliated individual generally needs an institutional or fiscal host. Live and archived calls appear in the same list across 26 pages — check status and deadline on each. Scope is global health and development as those partners define it; work outside that framing has no home here.

resources.name: Grants.gov
resources.summary: The single official listing of US federal discretionary funding opportunities across all agencies, searchable free of charge by keyword, agency, eligibility category and deadline.
resources.access: Free web search with no account; an account plus a SAM.gov registration for the applicant entity is required to submit. Saved searches can email you when matching opportunities post.
resources.notes: The site explicitly does not publish personal financial assistance — it is aimed at organisations, and most opportunities require an entity registration that takes weeks. A minority of notices list 'individuals' as an eligible applicant type; filter for those if you are unaffiliated. Non-US applicants are ineligible for most, though some agencies permit foreign institutions. Useful even when you cannot apply: reading funded solicitations tells you exactly how a US agency frames a problem.

resources.name: HFSP Postdoctoral Fellowships
resources.summary: Three-year, non-renewable fellowships in the life sciences with a living allowance, a research and travel allowance, and where applicable child, parental-leave and relocation allowances. Two tracks: Long-Term Fellowships for biology PhDs and Cross-Disciplinary Fellowships for PhDs from physics, chemistry, mathematics, engineering and computer science moving into biology.
resources.access: Two-stage application on the HFSP portal. For the 2027 cycle: LOI portal opens 12 March 2026, LOI initiation 5 May 2026, LOI submission 12 May 2026, full proposal 24 September 2026, outcome March 2027, fellowship starts between 1 April 2027 and 1 January 2028.
resources.notes: Nationality is unrestricted but mobility is mandatory: you cannot hold the fellowship in your country of nationality, and you must not have lived, studied or worked in the proposed host country for more than 12 months before it starts. An approved host institution and named supervisor are required at application, so the host search has to happen a year ahead. Allowance amounts vary by host country and are not fixed globally.

resources.name: Humboldt Research Fellowship
resources.summary: Alexander von Humboldt Foundation fellowship for non-German researchers to work in Germany: EUR 3,000 per month for 6-24 months for postdocs (doctorate within the last 4 years) or EUR 3,600 per month for 6-18 months for experienced researchers (doctorate within 12 years). Adds a health-insurance subsidy, travel costs, family allowances for accompanying dependants and an optional 2-4 month German language course; the stay can be split into up to three visits across three years.
resources.access: Direct online application by the researcher — no institutional nomination. Three calls a year closing 15 March, 15 July and 15 November; each round closes early once it reaches 800 applications, so submit well before the date.
resources.notes: You must secure a German host who signs a mentoring agreement and confirms facilities (the host separately receives a monthly research allowance of EUR 800 in the sciences, EUR 500 in the humanities), so finding the host is the real work and should start a year out. You must not have spent more than 90 days in Germany in the 18 months before submitting, which disqualifies anyone already there; German nationals qualify only after 10+ years abroad.

resources.name: ICML Financial Aid
resources.summary: Two award types for ICML 2026: an in-person award covering conference registration plus a seven-night hotel stay, and a virtual award covering virtual registration, aimed at people for whom attending would cause financial burden.
resources.access: Online application on the conference site. Opens 9 February 2026, closes 18 May 2026, decisions 1 June 2026; if you register before the 25 May early deadline and then win an award, registration is refunded.
resources.notes: No travel support is provided. Applicants must link their ICML.cc account email to their accepted papers. If you need a visa, register and request the invitation letter immediately rather than waiting for the aid decision — only registered participants get visa letters.

resources.name: ICTP (Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics)
resources.subcategory: programmes for scientists from developing countries
resources.summary: Trieste-based centre whose whole mandate is supporting scientists from developing countries, running the Postgraduate Diploma, master's programmes, PhD and sandwich-PhD arrangements, an Associateship scheme for repeat research visits, postdoctoral positions, laboratory placements and a large annual calendar of schools and workshops.
resources.access: Browse the Opportunities section and apply per programme; schools and workshops each publish their own application with a support request box.
resources.notes: The level of support differs sharply by activity — some schools cover travel and local costs for participants from developing countries, others only waive fees — so read the specific event page rather than assuming. Applications are competitive and typically require references from senior scientists.

resources.name: ICTP Postgraduate Diploma Programme
resources.summary: One academic year (1 September–31 August) in Trieste, Italy, in high energy/cosmology/astroparticle physics, condensed matter and statistical physics, mathematics, Earth system physics, or quantitative life sciences. Around ten scholarships per stream per year for candidates from developing countries, covering full tuition, an annual stipend and a travel grant.
resources.access: Online application via ICTP's e-applications portal with transcripts and degrees in English, English-proficiency evidence and two references from senior scientists; questions to diploma@ictp.it.
resources.notes: The programme page showed 'Call: To be announced' on 2026-08-28, so there was no open application at that date — watch the page rather than assuming a fixed annual window. Eligibility is tightly drawn: generally under 28, an MSc (or an exceptionally strong BSc) in physics, mathematics or a related field, fluency in English, and citizenship of a UN, UNESCO or IAEA member state. Tuition is free for every admitted student; the roughly ten scholarships per field, reserved for candidates from developing countries, are what cover travel and living costs. Self-funded candidates may attend if they can prove adequate resources.

resources.name: Idea Wild
resources.summary: Long-running programme (over 30 years) that provides field equipment rather than cash to conservation and biodiversity researchers, sourced through partnerships with suppliers including Vortex Optics, Burris Optics and Wildlife Acoustics. Applications are currently accepted from all countries.
resources.access: Online application form on the Idea Wild site listing the specific equipment you need and how it fits the project; questions to ideawild@ideawild.org.
resources.notes: Equipment only — no salaries, travel or consumables — and the maximum value is not published on the application page, so ask before building a wishlist. This is the fastest realistic route for a student in a low-income country who needs a camera trap, GPS unit or recorder and has no departmental budget.

resources.name: IMU Commission for Developing Countries
resources.summary: The International Mathematical Union's grant arm for developing countries: the Abel Visiting Scholar Program (one-month research visits abroad for graduate students), the IMU–Simons Research Fellowship (three-year Simons-funded collaborative research visits), the Breakout Graduate Fellowship, GRAID, a Conference Support Program for meetings held in developing countries, and the Volunteer Lecturer Program. 686 travel grants were awarded for ICM 2026.
resources.access: Each programme has its own application page and deadline under mathunion.org/cdc; several require nomination or endorsement by a mathematician or a host department.
resources.notes: Amounts are mostly not published on the overview page — read each programme page. The 686 ICM 2026 travel grants were awarded from roughly 2,000 applications worldwide. The only deadline live on 2026-08-28 was the Abel Visiting Scholar Program for Graduate Students, 15 September 2026 (recently extended). Some routes (Breakout Graduate Fellowship, Volunteer Lecturer Program, GRAID) run through institutions or nominators rather than direct individual application, so identify a sponsor early. Mathematics only.

resources.name: Kaggle Competitions
resources.summary: Free-to-enter machine-learning competitions, some sponsored with cash prize pools, alongside research and community competitions with no money attached. For an unaffiliated researcher this is one of the few routes where a laptop plus the free notebook tier can convert directly into both money and a citable public result.
resources.access: Create an account, accept the competition rules, then submit predictions or notebooks against a held-out leaderboard; free CPU/GPU/TPU notebook quotas are provided.
resources.notes: Most competitions carry no prize, and prize eligibility is governed per-competition — several exclude residents of sanctioned countries, require identity verification, and impose licence terms on winning solutions (sometimes including transferring rights to the sponsor). Read the rules tab before investing weeks. Expected value for a first-time entrant is close to zero money and considerable learning.

resources.name: Ko-fi
resources.subcategory: direct reader support for research programmes
resources.summary: Lightweight page for one-off tips, monthly memberships, commissions and digital-file sales, usable by an independent researcher who publishes a blog, dataset or newsletter and wants readers to pay for it directly.
resources.access: Web interface — create a page, connect Stripe or PayPal, and link it from your writing. A free account plus an optional paid 'Gold' tier with extra features.
resources.notes: Payment-processor fees always apply on top of whatever the platform charges; verify the current fee schedule before promising sponsors anything. Patreon is the larger alternative with more membership tooling but a higher platform cut. Income here tracks audience size, so it is a supplement to a research programme, not a foundation for one.

resources.name: LFX Mentorship
resources.summary: Paid remote mentorships on Linux Foundation and CNCF open-source projects. Mentee stipends start from a base of $6,000 USD adjusted by each country's purchasing-power-parity value, producing a range of $1,000 to $6,600, paid in instalments against evaluations and delivered milestones. Since 2019 more than 190 mentees have completed 96 mentorship programmes.
resources.access: Browse open mentorship projects on the platform at mentorship.lfx.dev, then apply to a specific project with a short proposal. Free to apply.
resources.notes: Payment is milestone-gated: miss evaluations or deliverables and instalments stop. The PPP adjustment means a mentee in a low-income country receives materially fewer nominal dollars than one in the United States for the same work. Projects are cloud-native and infrastructure software rather than scientific computing, so for a domain researcher the return is engineering skill and a public contribution record, not progress on their own research.

resources.name: Manifund
resources.summary: Public platform where anyone can post a funding proposal and have it funded by donors or by 'regrantors' — domain experts given delegated budgets. The site describes grants processed in days rather than months, and all proposals, comments and payouts are public.
resources.access: Create an account, publish a project page with budget and milestones, then solicit regrantors and donors directly. Impact-certificate rounds are also run periodically.
resources.notes: Funded work must fit a US charitable purpose (Manifund acts as fiscal sponsor). In practice the funded portfolio skews heavily toward AI safety, biosecurity and effective-altruism-adjacent projects; a proposal outside those areas is unlikely to find a regrantor. Everything you write is public, including a rejected ask.

resources.name: Marie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral Fellowships
resources.summary: Horizon Europe fellowships covering a living allowance, mobility allowance, family and special-needs allowances where applicable, plus research, training and networking costs. European Postdoctoral Fellowships run 1–2 years in an EU member state or associated country; Global Postdoctoral Fellowships run 2–3 years with 1–2 years outside Europe and a mandatory one-year return phase.
resources.access: Submitted jointly with a host organisation through the EU Funding & Tenders Portal; the annual call has a single deadline, usually in early autumn.
resources.notes: You need a PhD at the call deadline and at most eight years of post-PhD research experience (career breaks and non-research work are discounted). The mobility rule bites hardest: you must not have resided or worked in the host country for more than 12 months in the 36 months before the deadline, which rules out staying where you already are. A willing host supervisor is a prerequisite, so this is not a route for someone with no academic contacts. Success rates are typically well under one in five.

resources.name: Mohamed bin Zayed Species Conservation Fund
resources.summary: Grants for conservation of individual species — plants, animals and fungi — awarded without regional or taxonomic discrimination, prioritising critically endangered, endangered and data-deficient species. 3,274 grants have been awarded since 2009.
resources.access: Online application during one of three annual windows; open to individuals as well as organisations, worldwide.
resources.notes: Applications were closed on 2026-08-28. The grants page lists the next window as 15 September to 15 October 2026 (response late December), then 4-31 January 2027 (response late April 2027) and 1-31 May 2027 (response end of September 2027), and states that submission deadlines are inflexible. Grants are species-specific — a habitat or policy project without a clear focal species is a poor fit. Maximum award size is not stated on the grants page; read the guidelines in the portal at application.speciesconservation.org.

resources.name: National Geographic Society grants
resources.subcategory: grants to individuals without institutional affiliation
resources.summary: The Society funds individuals — explicitly not requiring an institutional affiliation — for projects in science, conservation, storytelling, education and technology, with applicants worldwide eligible and a minimum age of 18.
resources.access: All applications go through the National Geographic Funding Portal, against a specific request for proposals.
resources.notes: Important change: the Society has moved from an open-call model to time-bound, topic-specific RFPs, so the general 'Level I / Level II' open call that older guides describe no longer operates. As of 2026-08-28 only one RFP was listed — Understanding Ecosystem Dynamics and the Ecology of the Okavango River Basin (Angola, Namibia, Botswana), deadline 23 September 2026. You may lead only one project at a time, and demonstrated connection to the local context is weighted.

resources.name: NeurIPS Financial Assistance
resources.summary: Awards of complimentary conference registration and/or a prepaid hotel stay of up to seven nights at an affiliate hotel, prioritising student and junior-postdoc conference authors, then attendees with accessibility needs, affinity-group members, those in financial hardship and first-time attendees.
resources.access: Application form on the conference site during the assistance window; in the 2025 cycle it opened 1 September, closed 2 October (anywhere on Earth), with notification by 10 October.
resources.notes: Explicitly no travel support — no flights, no per diem, no expense reimbursement — so airfare and visa costs remain yours, which is the binding constraint for most applicants outside North America and Europe. Eligible authorship is limited to the main, Datasets & Benchmarks and Position Paper tracks; workshop and Creative AI papers do not count. The 2026 page had not yet been updated as of 2026-08-28; the terms above are the 2025 ones.

resources.name: NIH RePORTER
resources.summary: Free searchable repository of NIH-funded intramural and extramural research projects, with linked publications, patents and expenditure data, alongside sibling tools including the NIH Data Book and Awards by Location.
resources.access: Web interface with no registration; search by topic, PI, institution or study section, read funded abstracts, and export results. An API is available for bulk queries.
resources.notes: This is not a source of money — it is the best free way to see which programme officers and study sections actually fund your topic, how a successful specific-aims framing reads, and who your realistic collaborators are. US biomedical research only.

resources.name: NLnet Foundation (NGI Zero / Open Internet Stack)
resources.subcategory: grants to individuals for free/open-source work
resources.summary: Dutch foundation running open calls that fund individuals and small teams — not only institutions — to build free and open-source internet technology, including research software, privacy and security tooling. NLnet is currently winding down a decade of NGI Zero and transitioning to a new Open Internet Stack effort.
resources.access: Short online proposal form (a few pages, no institutional co-signature). Grants are milestone-based: you propose tasks and get paid as you deliver them.
resources.notes: Verified on 2026-08-28: there are no open calls right now. Calls reopen on 3 September 2026 with a deadline of 3 November 2026, 12:00 CEST. Funded work must be released under a free/open-source or open-hardware licence. The NGI-to-Open-Internet-Stack transition may change scope and eligibility, so read the applicant guide published with the September call rather than relying on older NGI Zero write-ups.

resources.name: NSF Award Search
resources.summary: Free, login-free search over US National Science Foundation awards, exposing project abstracts, award amounts, dates, programme officers and principal investigators across all NSF directorates.
resources.access: Web interface; results are downloadable in bulk (CSV/XML) for analysis, and the abstracts are public-domain US government text.
resources.notes: Like RePORTER, this is intelligence rather than funding. Most NSF programmes require a US institution as the awardee, so for unaffiliated and non-US researchers the value is entirely in reading how funded work is framed and identifying which groups have money for collaborators and students.

resources.name: NumFOCUS Small Development Grants
resources.summary: Microgrant programme awarding up to $10,000 per proposal for concrete work on NumFOCUS projects — usability improvements, documentation, community growth, accelerating a release — with a maximum of two grants per project per year and two rounds annually (proposals around 6 June and 17 October).
resources.access: Submit a proposal as a pull request / issue in the dedicated NumFOCUS GitHub repository during a round; off-cycle grants exist for time-sensitive work.
resources.notes: Only NumFOCUS fiscally sponsored or affiliated projects may apply (NumPy, pandas, Jupyter, Astropy, and so on), and only one proposal per project per cycle — so as an individual you need a maintainer to sponsor the work. Work can be performed anywhere subject to US export law. Round dates shift year to year; check the page for the current calendar.

resources.name: Open Collective
resources.summary: Transparent financial platform with fiscal hosts (Open Source Collective, Open Collective Europe and others) that give an unincorporated research project or community a legal home for money; the platform reports over $40M managed across more than 10,000 collectives.
resources.access: Web interface — apply to a fiscal host, then receive grants, donations and sponsorships and file expenses against the balance. Every transaction is public by default.
resources.notes: Hosts charge a percentage host fee that varies by host; check the specific host's page before committing. Full public transparency is a feature, not an option — line-item expenses including who was paid are visible. This is plumbing for receiving money, not a source of money.

resources.name: Outreachy
resources.subcategory: paid remote internships in open source
resources.summary: Three-month, fully remote, paid internships with a $7,000 stipend, in programming, research, UX, documentation, design, data science and more, for people facing under-representation, systemic bias or discrimination in the tech industry of their own country.
resources.access: Apply during an application window, then complete a public contribution period on a project before final selection. May 2026 cohort: applications 6–13 February 2026, contributions 17 March–15 April, internship 18 May–17 August 2026. December 2026 cohort: applications early-to-mid August 2026, contributions late September–late October, internship early December 2026–early March 2027.
resources.notes: The contribution period is real work done before you know whether you are accepted — budget several weeks. Eligibility is assessed against under-representation in your own country's tech industry, and there are time-commitment restrictions if you are simultaneously in full-time study or employment.

resources.name: OWSD (Organization for Women in Science for the Developing World)
resources.subcategory: fellowships for women scientists in the Global South
resources.summary: UNESCO-hosted organisation running PhD fellowships and an Early Career Fellowship for women scientists based in science-and-technology-lagging countries, plus a free international membership network.
resources.access: Applications through the OWSD portal during open calls; free membership is open to women scientists from developing countries and gives access to the network and calls.
resources.notes: Award amounts, current call status and country lists could not be confirmed on 2026-08-28 — several OWSD programme pages returned errors, so verify on the site before planning around a figure you have read elsewhere. Eligibility is restricted by gender, nationality and current country of work; the Early Career Fellowship additionally requires an institutional base to host the grant.

resources.name: Perimeter Scholars International (PSI)
resources.subcategory: fully funded master's in theoretical physics
resources.summary: A one-year condensed master's in theoretical physics at Perimeter Institute in Waterloo, Canada, awarding an MSc from the University of Waterloo. Full scholarships are extended to up to all accepted students and cover tuition, a living stipend, accommodation, meals, health insurance, necessary IT equipment and travel support.
resources.access: Apply through Perimeter's admissions portal; applications for the next cohort open in October 2026. Funding is decided as part of admission — there is no separate scholarship application.
resources.notes: Benefits are provided in kind with no cash value. Students are expected to also apply for external scholarships they qualify for, and any award obtained is partly applied against programme costs. Admission is highly competitive and the year is deliberately intense; it is a launchpad into a theory PhD rather than a terminal degree.

resources.name: Prototype Fund
resources.summary: German public funding line that supports individual developers and very small teams — not companies or universities — to build open-source software prototypes in the public interest over a fixed six-month period.
resources.access: Rounds with fixed deadlines; a short German-language application describing the prototype, the team and the milestones.
resources.notes: Residency in Germany is required, and applications are effectively in German. The site returned HTTP 403 to automated checks on 2026-08-28 and the fund's public backing has changed hands in recent years, so confirm the current round, funder and amount on the site before relying on it — do not plan against remembered figures.

resources.name: Schmidt Science Fellows
resources.summary: Postdoctoral fellowship supporting a deliberate pivot into a new discipline, for PhDs in natural sciences, engineering, mathematics or computing.
resources.access: You cannot apply directly. Your PhD-awarding institution must be one of the programme's nominating partner organisations and must nominate you; contact your graduate school's fellowships office early. For the current cycle the PhD must be completed, including a successful defence, between 1 May 2026 and 30 June 2027.
resources.notes: Listed here mainly so you can rule it out quickly: the nomination gate means that if your university is not a partner there is no route in, which excludes most researchers at poorly resourced institutions outright. Clinical MD-PhD, veterinary-PhD, and social science, political science or economics PhDs are generally ineligible. Stipend figures are not published on the eligibility page.

resources.name: Sovereign Tech Agency
resources.subcategory: public funding for critical open-source infrastructure
resources.summary: German government-owned body that invests public money in foundational open-source software, with programme lines including the Sovereign Tech Fund (investments in critical components), a Fellowship for Maintainers on a 'maintainer-in-residence' model that pays individuals, plus Resilience and Challenge tracks. Reported budgets: €13M in 2022 and around €22M in 2023.
resources.access: Programme pages carry the current calls and intake forms; the Fellowship is the line aimed at individual maintainers rather than organisations.
resources.notes: The agency's own site returned HTTP 403 to automated checks on 2026-08-28, so the programme details above come from secondary documentation — confirm current calls, amounts and eligibility on the site before planning around it. Funding targets infrastructure the German and European digital economy depends on; a niche scientific package with few downstream users is a poor fit.

resources.name: The Company of Biologists Travelling Fellowships
resources.summary: Awards of up to GBP 3,000 for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers to make a collaborative research visit to another laboratory, offered through the journals Development, Journal of Cell Science and Journal of Experimental Biology. Two rounds in 2026: 7 August (travel starting after 21 September) and 23 October (travel starting after 7 December).
resources.access: Direct online application to the scheme run by the relevant journal — no nationality restriction and no institutional grants office required.
resources.notes: Only one person per laboratory may apply in a given round; travel must begin within six months of the award and must not start before the decision date, so there is no retrospective funding. A recipient may win only once every two years across all three journals. Your project has to sit within the scope of the journal you apply through, which rules out most non-organismal and non-cell-biology work.

resources.name: The Rufford Foundation
resources.summary: UK foundation funding nature-conservation projects and pilot studies led by individuals, with a reported 6,841 projects supported across 152 countries over two decades. One of the most accessible funders for a field researcher with no institutional grant office.
resources.access: Apply through the Rufford application portal at apply.ruffordsmallgrants.org; the ladder is designed so that a completed small grant qualifies you to apply for the next tier.
resources.notes: Grant-tier amounts are not published on the main site pages — read the current guidance in the portal rather than relying on remembered figures. Scope is conservation in developing countries, and applicants working in high-income countries are generally out of scope. Grants are modest and field-cost oriented; salaries are usually not the point.

resources.name: TWAS Fellowships
resources.summary: The world's largest South–South fellowship programme: roughly 160 PhD and 100 postdoctoral fellowships per year, placing early-career researchers from developing countries at host institutions in other developing countries through partnerships with national science agencies.
resources.access: Apply through the TWAS online portal; you must first secure a preliminary acceptance letter from a host institution in the partner country.
resources.notes: One application per calendar year, and taking a TWAS fellowship bars you from visiting another institution under a different TWAS programme that year. The preliminary acceptance letter is the real bottleneck — start contacting prospective hosts months before the deadline. Terms (stipend, travel, family allowances) are set by the partner country, not TWAS, and differ substantially.

resources.name: TWAS Research Grants Programme (Basic Sciences, individuals)
resources.summary: Grants of up to USD 30,000 (with equipment and supplies capped at USD 20,000) to individual early-career researchers in biology, chemistry, mathematics and physics, funding scientific equipment, consumable supplies and specialised literature.
resources.access: Online application through the TWAS portal during an open call.
resources.notes: TWAS states that no call will open in 2026 — the last deadline was 3 April 2025, so treat this as a 2027-or-later target and watch the deadlines page. Eligibility is narrow: nationals of developing countries, PhD held, age 45 or under, employed at a university or research institute in one of the 66 science-and-technology-lagging countries TWAS lists, and not already holding a TWAS or OWSD grant. It explicitly does not cover salaries, student pay, field expenses, travel, laptops, tablets, drones or laboratory animals.

resources.name: UKRI Funding Finder
resources.summary: Official searchable index of funding opportunities across the nine UK Research and Innovation councils; 141 opportunities were listed on 2026-08-28, filterable by status (open, closed, upcoming), council, funding type (fellowship, grant, loan, other) and opening or closing date.
resources.access: Free web search, no account needed. Each opportunity page carries the full call document, eligibility text and deadline; submission itself goes through the UKRI Funding Service with a UK host organisation.
resources.notes: Almost every opportunity requires the applicant to be based at a UK research organisation eligible for that council's funding, or to be a UK-registered business, so for an unaffiliated or non-UK researcher this is intelligence rather than money. The useful free product is the call documents themselves: they state assessment criteria explicitly, which is rare and worth reading before writing any proposal anywhere.

resources.name: Wikimedia Research Fund
resources.summary: Annual fund for research on Wikimedia projects, open to individuals, groups and organisations across disciplines: Types 1 and 3 are $2,000–$50,000, Type 2 is $50,000–$150,000 with a $75,000 per-year cap.
resources.access: Letter of intent then full proposal, submitted through OpenReview. In the 2025–26 round the LOI deadline was 16 January 2026, LOI decisions 6 February, full proposals 3 April, final notifications 1 May 2026.
resources.notes: No round was open on 2026-08-28. In the 2025-26 round the single-stage deadline of 3 April 2026 covered all Type 3 proposals as well as advanced Type 1-2, with final notifications on 1 May 2026 and funded work able to start from 1 July 2026 — so Type 3 is not a rolling route. Applicants may hold at most three open grants (organisations five), the minimum request is over USD 2,000, applications must be in English, and you cannot have been a Wikimedia Foundation employee or contractor in the last 24 months. Review is public on OpenReview.

resources.name: Zindi
resources.summary: AI and data-science challenge platform and professional network for emerging markets, launched in 2018, with members across more than 185 countries. Challenges are posted by companies, NGOs and government bodies, carry cash prizes and a public leaderboard record; Zindi reports that 1 in 5 users got a data-science or AI job through their profile.
resources.access: Free account, then join a challenge, download the data and submit predictions against a held-out leaderboard. Hackathons and no-prize learning challenges also run continuously.
resources.notes: The zindi.africa domain now redirects to zindi.world. Prize pools, eligibility and country restrictions are set per challenge — read the rules tab, because some restrict prizes to residents of specific African countries and some require the winning solution to be licensed to the sponsor. Datasets are smaller and problems more applied than Kaggle's, which means less crowding but also smaller purses; for a newcomer the realistic payoff is a portfolio and a network, not income.

resources.name: Recurse Center
resources.summary: A free 6- or 12-week self-directed programming retreat, available in person in Brooklyn (two floors, open 24/7, core hours 11am–5pm) or fully remote, with new batches starting every six weeks. It is free because companies pay recruiting fees, not because participants do.
resources.access: Written application plus two pair-programming interviews; no degree, no CV screen, and researchers using it to build computational skills or a research tool are a normal fit.
resources.notes: Free to attend but not free to live through — you cover your own housing and living costs for the batch, which is the real barrier. Recurse has historically offered need-based living-expense grants for people from groups under-represented in programming; the grants page did not resolve on 2026-08-28, so ask admissions directly rather than assuming. The remote batch removes the New York cost problem entirely.

resources.name: Rising Scholars (formerly AuthorAID)
resources.subcategory: research-writing and grant-proposal training for the Global South
resources.summary: INASP's rebranded AuthorAID network: a free global community of more than 14,000 researchers from 175 countries, offering free online courses in research communication, proposal writing and community-engaged research on its Moodle platform, a library of nearly 900 resources, and mentoring matches between early-career and experienced researchers.
resources.access: Free registration on the site, then enrol in a course, browse the resource library, or request or offer mentoring. Courses are online and asynchronous.
resources.notes: The old authoraid.info domain now 301-redirects here, so older links, syllabi and citations still name the previous brand. It awards no research money itself — the value is that the proposal-writing course and the mentor matching are aimed squarely at making a first grant application competitive. Course cohorts run on a schedule, so you may wait for the next intake. Material is pitched at researchers in low- and middle-income countries.

resources.name: NASA Citizen Science
resources.summary: Catalogue of 46 active NASA citizen-science projects open to anyone; more than 650 NASA citizen scientists have co-authored peer-reviewed publications, making this a documented route to authorship without any institutional affiliation.
resources.access: Pick a project from the catalogue and join through its own site; most need only a smartphone or laptop, a few (asteroid occultations, exoplanet transits) want a telescope. Subscribe to updates by emailing do-nasa-science-join@lists.nasa.gov with 'Subscribe' in the subject.
resources.notes: Co-authorship is real but not automatic: it depends on sustained, substantial contribution and on each project team's authorship policy. There is no stipend — this buys credibility and a publication record, not income.

resources.name: Zooniverse
resources.summary: The largest people-powered research platform, with projects spanning astronomy, biology, climate, history and physics, and a long record of peer-reviewed publications produced from volunteer classifications since 2007.
resources.access: Volunteer on any project with a free account. Researchers can build their own project at no cost with the Zooniverse Project Builder, submit it for review, launch it, then download the aggregated classifications.
resources.notes: The Project Builder is the underrated half: an unaffiliated researcher with an image or transcription dataset can get thousands of human labels for free, which no budget would otherwise buy. Projects must pass Zooniverse review before launch, and attracting volunteers to a new project requires active community work — a launched project is not a staffed one.
